newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMU chances best with homogeneous group - Tietmeyer.
newsitem.headline: EMU chances best with homogeneous group - Tietmeyer.

text.p: European economic and monetary union (EMU) stands the best chance of succeeding if it is led by a "homogeneous" group of states, Hans Tietmeyer, President of the German Bundesbank, said on Monday.
Tietmeyer told an audience of bankers that the Maastricht Treaty's convergence criteria must be met strictly and sustainably to guarantee "a minimum degree of homogeneity" under EMU.

"Such a relatively homogeneous group of participants opens up good chances that the euro will be lastingly stable and the currency union will last without suffering internal strains," Tietmeyer said according to a text of his speech released in advance of delivery.
Tietmeyer made no direct comment on which countries he considered should be allowed to join the EMU club when European leaders decide on membership in a year's time.
Both Germany and France last week denied reports that they were hatching a plot to exclude heavily-indebted Italy, and with it Spain, from joining the starting EMU lineup.
But Tietmeyer did make clear what he believed countries must do to create a solid foundation for the planned currency.
He said fulfilling all of the Maastricht criteria was important, and he favoured a "strict and narrow" interpretation of the treaty in judging which countries can join EMU.
The criteria must also be fulfilled "sustainably and credibly" rather than achieved through one-off book-keeping tricks, he added.

"A responsible treatment of the criteria when selecting members will give the euro a fair chance," he said. "Political prestige considerations will not help when we are talking about economic and stability capabilities."
He warned that monetary union needed to be solidly based, because it would tend to increase economic tensions between countries.
Continental European countries face common challenges of high unemployment, strained welfare states, ageing populations and the shift from industry to services, he said.

Those would have to be dealt with anyway, but countries joining EMU will have to cope with them without having the option of resorting to changes in national exchange rates or easy migration of labour to more prosperous European regions.
"Countries in the monetary union must have the strength to be able to keep up, even if they are hit particularly hard by structural changes in particular markets and sectors," he said.
"If member economies drifted apart, then the currency union would strengthen such a tendency."
Tietmeyer also said the Bundesbank was operating on the assumption that the euro's launch would go ahead on schedule at the start of 1999.
"That is the current orientation," Tietmeyer said.
